title: There's a one-word fix for natural sort in JavaScript, and it's off by default
assumption: Fixing "file10 sorts before file2" requires writing your own digit-splitting comparator.

input.description: The same filename-sorting problem as the plain natural-sort exhibit, this time looking for the fix rather than the bug.

what_goes_wrong: Passing { numeric: true } as an option to localeCompare correctly returns ["file1.txt", "file2.txt", "file10.txt"] with no custom parsing code at all — but it is not the default for localeCompare, not the default for Array.prototype.sort(), and has no equivalent option anywhere in Python's standard library sorted(); Python's locale.strxfrm (the one built-in collation hook Python has) does not implement it either and returns the same wrong lexicographic order as a plain sort.
why: ECMA-402 (the Intl part of JavaScript) defines a numeric collation option (the Unicode locale extension "kn") that makes the collator compare runs of decimal digits by their numeric value instead of character by character, and String.prototype.localeCompare accepts the same options object as Intl.Collator. It is opt-in because it is a tailoring on top of the default Unicode Collation Algorithm ordering, not the default. Python ships no Unicode collation implementation: locale.strxfrm only applies whatever collation the operating system's locale provides, and the common C-library locales have no numeric-run option, so in Python the digit-run comparison has to be hand-written.

repros.code:
const files = ["file10.txt", "file2.txt", "file1.txt"];
console.log(files.slice().sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b, undefined, { numeric: true })));

fix: In JavaScript, pass { numeric: true } to localeCompare (or construct one Intl.Collator with that option and reuse its compare for the whole sort, which is faster). It only treats runs of digits as non-negative integers: signs, decimal points and thousands separators are still compared as characters. In Python, write a natural-sort key that splits each string on digit runs with re.split(r"(\d+)", s) and converts the digit groups to int, since there is no built-in numeric collation to opt into.
